transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Cobalt Head of ML), Ethan Brooks (Cobalt Infra), Lena Morales (Cobalt Product)

Auto-generated summary: Intro catalog showcase + bench crossover. Some parts of the transcript may be mis-attributed or garbled.

00:00 Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate it. Quick agenda, we'll do a short 10 minute catalog walkthrough, then Jordan will demo the bench crossover view and compatibility matrix, and we'll leave time for Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
00:28 Priya Nair: Yep that works, thanks Maya. Wanted to flag up front our success criteria are strict latency under 120ms p50 for our chat endpoint and unit cost targets under $0.0008 per token at our expected QPS, and we also have PII retention rules so private deployment is possible.
00:46 Maya Patel: Got it, that's helpful. Jordan, I'll hand over.
00:52 Jordan Lee: cool thanks. So starting in the catalog you'll see we group open models by architecture and by verified performance. I'll pull up a shortlist we curated for LLM-chat use cases with seq lengths of around 512. Excuse my mouse, ok visible?
01:18 Ethan Brooks: we can see it, yeah. Quick question — is the verified performance based on your internal bench or public numbers?
01:26 Jordan Lee: Mostly our internal bench runs — we run microbenchmarks on throughput/latency across target GPUs with our kernel selection logic. We also annotate community scores and evals. The "bench crossover" view ties model perf to the compatibility matrix — that shows which kernels, quantization profiles, and hardware combos are recommended.
01:50 Priya Nair: When you say quantization profiles, do you support LLMQ8 / 4-bit per-tensor stuff? We need to preserve quality for medical text.
02:03 Jordan Lee: yes we have multiple quant profiles; we typically present a quality delta and recommended fallback. For sensitive text you'd probably start with q4f then test q8 on lower-tier traffic. The catalog will show expected quality regression estimates from our evals but we always recommend a short A/B on your prompts.
02:26 Lena Morales: can you show the cost math for a selected model? Like if we pick model X what's cost at our QPS?
02:34 Jordan Lee: sure, I'll enable the cost overlay. So model A (open-llm-7b-variant) at ded skew runs around 90ms p50 on an A100-80g with q4f and estimated $0.00065 per token after batching and KV cache for our sample trace. If you look at model B it's slightly cheaper but latency creeps up.
03:05 Priya Nair: those numbers look promising, the delta between the two models is small but how confident are you in the p50 numbers for our traffic pattern which has many short-turn exchanges?
03:18 Jordan Lee: good point — short exchanges favor low-latency kernels and lower batch sizes. We can run a focused microbenchmark using your session distribution; that's what Jordan will do as an action item. (laughs)
03:31 Priya Nair: (laughs) fair.
03:34 Maya Patel: I also wanted to highlight routing policies — you can set policy to prefer lower-cost variants for background tasks and pin a high-accuracy variant for the interactive path. That way you meet both cost and quality needs.
03:52 Ethan Brooks: on private deployment — we need to understand network topology. Do you support VPC peering and customer-managed NAT? Also KMS integration for key rotation, SOC2 logs?
04:07 Jordan Lee: yes we support VPC peering, private control plane, and HSM/KMS integrations. We produce audit logs with per-request metadata and token-level cost breakdowns. For SOC2 we provide our compliance pack; I'll attach that in the follow-up.
04:25 Priya Nair: great. On the compatibility matrix, I saw a "kernel mismatch" flag earlier — what does that mean in practice?
04:33 Jordan Lee: it's basically where the model's operator pattern triggers a suboptimal kernel on a particular runtime/hw combo — we surface that so you don't pick a model that looks good on paper but will regress at scale. In the bench crossover we show fallback hardware or fallback model variants.
04:50 Lena Morales: do you have a recommended shortlist for us given our latency / cost targets?
04:57 Jordan Lee: yes, we generated a top 4 list: model-A, model-C, model-D, and a distilled variant model-D-lite. Each row links to bench results, sample evals on your domain (synthetic medical prompts), and a compatibility tag.
05:18 Priya Nair: what about caching — KV cache warmup on short sessions is a concern for us since first token latency matters.
05:27 Jordan Lee: we do prefix caching and also an option for hot-entry cache where frequent session prefixes get pinned; that reduces cold start considerably. For very short sessions, small batch sizes plus kernel selection is usually best.
05:44 Maya Patel: quick demo now of the bench crossover panel, I'm going to show a heatmap where rows are models and columns are hardware+quant combos. The color encodes p50 latency and a small overlay shows per-token cost.
06:05 Jordan Lee: yeah there's also a filter to mark models with clinical evals or redwood-verified low hallucination scores which I think matters for Cobalt.
06:18 Priya Nair: hallu — hallucination — yes that's critical. Can you quantify the hallucination metric? Is it human-eval based or automated?
06:27 Jordan Lee: currently a mix — we run automated checks for factual consistency, then sample human evals for edge cases. We'll provide the evaluation rubric.
06:38 Ethan Brooks: another infra question — when you recommend an A100-80g node, is that per replica? How does autoscaling interact with warm KV caches?
06:48 Jordan Lee: A100-80g runner is a per-replica config. Autoscaling can be set to keep a minimum number warm to preserve KV state or scale-to-zero for cost savings. We recommend a small warm pool for low-latency services.
07:06 Priya Nair: can you show an example prompt set run-through? I can paste one now.
07:12 Lena Morales: I'll paste a short sample set in the chat, three prompts, token lengths about 30-120.
07:25 Jordan Lee: got it, pasting. Running an inline sample eval — results coming... apologies if the transcription lags.
07:46 Jordan Lee: first model A answers show strong fidelity, p50 88ms, quality score 0.92 on our rubric; model C p50 110ms quality 0.90; model D-lite p50 75ms but quality 0.82.
08:09 Priya Nair: that aligns with what we need. How easy is it to pin a canary rollout for a small percent of traffic? We want to run canary on 5% traffic for 2 weeks.
08:21 Maya Patel: very straightforward — the console has rollout rules, canary percent by route, and automatic rollback if quality regressions exceed a threshold. We can tie regression alerts to your prompt set.
08:35 Ethan Brooks: on the matter of SSO and RBAC — we need role separation for infra vs product people, ideally SCIM provisioning.
08:44 Maya Patel: yep we support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and granular roles.
08:50 Priya Nair: who typically owns the bench runs during pilot, Redwood or customer?
08:55 Jordan Lee: typically a joint effort — we run the initial set to validate model mapping, then we hand over the bench harness and run with your prompts; we can also run the private pilot within your VPC if you prefer.
09:06 Priya Nair: private pilot inside VPC would be ideal. Any network egress concerns?
09:12 Jordan Lee: if you choose private deployment the control plane traffic is limited; we can run air-gapped or with a customer-managed proxy. We'll share the network diagram in the follow-up.
09:23 Lena Morales: what's the timeline for ramp — if we sign a pilot next week, when can we expect pilot results?
09:29 Maya Patel: typical pilot is 2 weeks for initial benching and small traffic canary; results in about 10 business days from pilot kick-off.
09:36 Priya Nair: ok good.
09:38 Jordan Lee: small nit on model naming — the catalog has model-A/B/C placeholders but our bench workbook will map to upstream model repo names so you can reproduce locally.
09:49 Ethan Brooks: any blockers on our side? We need to give you a sample of real prompts, expected concurrency, and preference for on-prem vs VPC.
09:58 Priya Nair: we'll do that. Also pricing — can you give baseline pricing for hosted vs dedicated vs private?
10:05 Maya Patel: quick snapshot: hosted is usage-based with token and embedding units; dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commit and lower unit cost; private is enterprise license plus infra. I'll attach an anonymized pricing sheet. Exact numbers depend on model selection and quantization.
10:24 Priya Nair: fine.
10:28 Maya Patel: circling back to the compatibility matrix, you can download it as CSV and it contains flags for kernel mismatch, quantization risk, recommended hardware, and bench links. That CSV will be useful for your procurement and infra planning.
10:45 Jordan Lee: also note we have a "fallback policy" — if primary variant can't meet SLO the router will send traffic to a compatible variant, we can tune that to avoid user-facing errors.
10:58 Priya Nair: good.
11:02 Lena Morales: one last product question — how do you handle model rollbacks if an eval suddenly drops?
11:07 Jordan Lee: the rollout engine supports automatic rollback and also can trigger a snapshot of prompts that failed so you can triage. We also surface the token-level trace for debugging.
11:20 Priya Nair: that helps.
11:23 Maya Patel: ok we'll open it up for some questions — feel free to interrupt.
11:28 Ethan Brooks: curious if you support hybrid routing — a portion on-prem and a portion hosted? For regulatory reasons some PII must remain on-prem.
11:37 Jordan Lee: yes hybrid routing is supported; we can route sensitive routes to a private deployment and send non-sensitive to hosted endpoints. The console will show cost implications.
11:48 Priya Nair: what about model updates — if an upstream model changes behavior, do you support pinned model versions?
11:55 Maya Patel: yes, you can pin versions and we also support canary tests when a new seed lands. We keep older artifacts for rollback.
12:08 Lena Morales: ok can we see an example of the CSV export?
12:12 Jordan Lee: downloading now, sharing link in chat (link: drive.redwood/bench-export-ct).
12:25 Priya Nair: got it.
12:28 Maya Patel: any final concerns?
12:31 Priya Nair: only that we want to validate hallucination sensitivity on the clinical prompts — we'll share a focused set.
12:37 Maya Patel: perfect, that'll be part of the pilot.
12:40 Jordan Lee: I'll queue the latency pass against your session distribution once you upload the prompts and QPS numbers.
12:48 Ethan Brooks: timeline check again — we aim to have pilot kickoff the week of Dec 28, results mid-Jan.
12:56 Maya Patel: noted. I'll send the calendar invite once we have confirmation.
13:00 Priya Nair: thanks everyone, appreciate the demo.
13:04 Maya Patel: thanks all. End.

Note: timestamps above are relative conversation markers not exact sec-by-sec alignment; transcription contains occasional word swaps ("hallu" for hallucination) and truncated names.
